citation: Pencavel J. (2014) The Productivity of Working Hours. IZA DP 8129; Economic Journal 125 (2015) 2052-2076
design: Historical observational; group fixed effects; spline in hours
population: UK WWI munition workers (mostly women), HMWC records
estimate_as_stated: Below 49 weekly hours output proportional to hours (log-linear delta1 = unity); output max ~63h; 48h no-Sunday week output 1.4% above 70h week. Derived theta~0 below ~48h
quality_note: No policy experiment; manual work 1916; strong reason for small offset at 30-39h; low generalisability to services

citation: Collewet M. & Sauermann J. (2017) Working hours and productivity. Labour Economics 47:96-106 doi:10.1016/j.labeco.2017.03.006
design: Within-worker panel; scheduling-driven hours variation; individual+time FE
estimate_as_stated: 1% more hours -> 0.9% more calls answered. Derived theta~0.1
quality_note: Good internal identification; single firm/task; short-run fatigue only; directly in 20-35h range

citation: Gubian A., Jugnot S., Lerais F., Passeron V. (2004) Les effets de la RTT sur l'emploi: des simulations ex ante aux evaluations ex post. Economie et Statistique 376-377:25-54
design: Official DARES ex post evaluation; firm comparisons; productivity inferred assuming output neutrality
population: French firms adopting 35h (Aubry I/Robien aided; Aubry II)
estimate_as_stated: Aubry I: >10% effective hours cut, +6-7% jobs, hourly productivity gains ~4-5%; 'gains de productivite apparente ... 40 a 50 % de la baisse de la duree' vs one-third ex ante; economy-wide effective cut <5% (DARES) to >6% (national accounts); ~350,000 jobs 1998-2002. Derived theta~0.4-0.5
quality_note: Output not observed (assumed neutral); self-selected subsidised firms; agency self-evaluation; upper-end for first ~10% cut

citation: Crepon B., Leclair M., Roux S. (2004) RTT, productivite et emploi: nouvelles estimations sur donnees d'entreprises. Economie et Statistique 376-377:55-89
design: Firm-level comparison 1997-2000, selection on observables (OLS, matching)
population: French firms: Aubry I aided vs firms at 39h
estimate_as_stated: Aubry I aided vs 39h firms: TFP (headcount-based) -3.68% (se 0.31) vs nominal hours cut 10.2%; VA/L -4.89%; employment +9.91%; VA +5.02%; K +4.20%. Derived theta~0.52 (VA/head) to 0.64 (TFP)
quality_note: Pre-trends acknowledged; hours poorly measured; volunteer subsidised firms; includes capital deepening

citation: Asai K., Lopes M.C., Tondini A. (2024) Firm-Level Effects of Reductions in Working Hours. Working paper (merges Asai 2022; Lopes & Tondini 2022)
design: Difference-in-differences; matched employer-employee data; unexpected national reform
estimate_as_stated: Hours -2.5h (-6%); +6% hourly wage -> ~-2% employment, -9% total hours, -4% sales; hourly labour productivity (sales/hour) +4.4%; larger in capital-intensive sectors. Derived theta~0.7 (partly capital substitution)
quality_note: Credible design; working paper; high starting hours; sales/hour mixes capital and composition

citation: Batut C., Garnero A., Tondini A. (2023) The Employment Effects of Working Time Reductions: Sector-Level Evidence from European Reforms. Industrial Relations 62(3):217-232
design: Sector-level DiD exploiting 5 national reforms and initial exposure; EU KLEMS + EU-LFS
population: 23 European countries x 32 industries 1995-2007 (excl. health, education, agriculture)
estimate_as_stated: Panel A with controls (log): hours/employee -0.013***, total hours -0.036**, employment -0.023 (se 0.027), VA -0.025 (0.022), VA/hour +0.012 (0.022). Panel B: hours/emp -0.059***, VA/hour +0.169 (0.119). Full work-sharing rejected. Derived theta point ~0.9 but CI ~[-2,+4]
quality_note: Best multi-country design; relative sector effects only; productivity underpowered

citation: Park W. & Park Y. (2019) When Less is More: The Impact of the Regulation on Standard Workweek on Labor Productivity in South Korea. J. Policy Analysis and Management 38(3):681-705 doi:10.1002/pam.22136
design: Difference-in-differences on phased rollout
estimate_as_stated: Policy reduced per-worker hours but increased per-worker output; +1.5% annual output per worker (plants 10+ employees, KDI version). Derived theta>1
quality_note: Long baseline hours (above Pencavel threshold); manufacturing; not transferable to 39->30h

citation: Hunt J. (1999) Has Work-Sharing Worked in Germany? QJE 114(1):117-148 (NBER WP 5724, 1996)
design: Industry panel (201 manufacturing industries) + GSOEP separations; standard hours from union agreements
estimate_as_stated: WP: 1h standard-hours cut -> employment +0.3-0.7% (Arbeiter), +0.2-0.3% (Angestellte), aggregate at most 1.1%; worker-hours -2-3%. QJE abstract: work-sharing 'may have reduced employment in the period 1984-1994'; hourly wage rose enough to offset hours decline
quality_note: Conditional on sales (scale effect partly removed); bargained not mandated; versions differ

citation: Crepon B. & Kramarz F. (2002) Employed 40 Hours or Not Employed 39: Lessons from the 1982 Mandatory Reduction of the Workweek. JPE 110(6):1355-1389
design: Worker-level panel; treated = working 40h/overtime in 1981
estimate_as_stated: Employment losses from the one-hour cut 'between 2% and 4%'; minimum-wage workers hit hardest
quality_note: Strong worker-level identification; separations only (no hiring/GE); monthly pay held constant

citation: Chemin M. & Wasmer E. (2009) Using Alsace-Moselle Local Laws to Build a Difference-in-Differences Estimation Strategy of the Employment Effects of the 35-Hour Workweek Regulation in France. JOLE 27(4):487-524 doi:10.1086/605426
design: Regional DiD/DDD using weaker implementation in Alsace-Moselle
estimate_as_stated: No significant employment difference vs rest of France; casts doubt on regulation's effectiveness
quality_note: Credible regional identification; partial treatment contrast; effect sizes not read

citation: Estevao M. & Sa F. (2008) The 35-hour workweek in France: Straightjacket or welfare improvement? Economic Policy 23(55):417-463
design: DiD on staggered timing (large firms 2000, small 2002)
estimate_as_stated: 'aggregate employment was unaffected but labour turnover increased'; women may have benefited, managers negative welfare
quality_note: Good timing-based design; limited to employment/welfare, no productivity

citation: Raposo P.S. & van Ours J.C. (2010) How working time reduction affects jobs and wages. Economics Letters 106(1):61-63
design: Worker-level DiD
estimate_as_stated: Reduced job separation and increased hourly wages for affected workers (monthly earnings ~constant); workers below 40h more likely to lose job
quality_note: Separations only; spillovers on non-treated

citation: Kawaguchi D., Naito H., Yokoyama I. (2017) Assessing the effects of reducing standard hours: Regression discontinuity evidence from Japan. JJIE 43:59-76 doi:10.1016/j.jjie.2016.12.002; ESRI DP 202 (2008)
design: Regression discontinuity / establishment data
estimate_as_stated: Hours fell, monthly wages and bonuses did not; policy 'did not contribute to job creation'. ESRI WP: 1h legal cut -> 0.14h actual cut; new-graduate recruitment suppressed
quality_note: Good design; weak pass-through of legal to actual hours

citation: Sanchez R. (2013) Do reductions of standard hours affect employment transitions?: Evidence from Chile. Labour Economics 20:24-37 doi:10.1016/j.labeco.2012.10.001
design: Difference-in-differences, isolated policy change
estimate_as_stated: 'no significant effects of a reduction of standard hours on employment transitions and a significant effect on hourly wages'
quality_note: Clean policy; long baseline hours; transitions not levels

citation: Autonomy & Alda (2021) Going Public: Iceland's journey to a shorter working week
design: Trial report; pre/post with some control units; mixed qualitative/quantitative
population: ~2,500 Icelandic public-sector workers 2015-19 (offices, playschools, social services, hospitals); 40h->35-36h
estimate_as_stated: 'Productivity and service provision remained the same or improved across the majority of trial workplaces'; national rollout: 'more staff had to be hired', 4.2 bn ISK/yr, two-thirds in healthcare
quality_note: Advocacy report; no common metric; small selected units; healthcare hiring cost is the key policy fact (itself cited from press)

citation: Autonomy et al. (2023) The results are in: The UK's four-day week pilot
design: Pre/post, no control group; firm admin data + employee surveys
estimate_as_stated: Hours 38->34/week (self-report); revenue +1.4% (23 firms), +34.5% vs prior period (24 firms); headcount -1.3% (34 firms); sick days 2.0->0.7/employee/month; resignations 2->0.8 per 100; trends not statistically significant. Naive theta~1
quality_note: Severe self-selection; nominal revenue not output; <half reported; advocate-run; not usable economy-wide

citation: Rogers A.E., Hwang W.T., Scott L.D., Aiken L.H., Dinges D.F. (2004) The working hours of hospital staff nurses and patient safety. Health Affairs 23(4):202-212 doi:10.1377/hlthaff.23.4.202
design: Logbook observational study
estimate_as_stated: Error risk significantly increased with shifts >12h, overtime, or >40h/week ('For those shifts longer than 12.5 hours, the error rate increased notably')
quality_note: Observational; concerns long hours, not cuts below 39h

citation: Dall'Ora C. et al. (2015) Association of 12 h shifts and nurses' job satisfaction, burnout and intention to leave. BMJ Open 5(9):e008331
design: Cross-sectional survey
estimate_as_stated: Shifts >=12h vs <=8h: emotional exhaustion aOR 1.26; job dissatisfaction aOR 1.40; intention to leave aOR 1.29
quality_note: Cross-sectional; shift length not weekly-hours cut

citation: Griffiths P. et al. (2014) Nurses' shift length and overtime working in 12 European countries: the association with perceived quality of care and patient safety. Medical Care doi:10.1097/MLR.0000000000000233
design: Cross-sectional survey
estimate_as_stated: Shifts >=12h: poor/failing safety OR 1.41; care left undone RR 1.13; overtime: poor safety OR 1.67
quality_note: Self-reported quality; long-shift context

citation: Aiken L.H. et al. (2014) Nurse staffing and education and hospital mortality in nine European countries. The Lancet (RN4CAST) (volume/pages unverified)
design: Retrospective observational; GEE with risk adjustment
population: 422,730 surgical patients, 300 hospitals, 9 countries; 26,516 nurses surveyed
estimate_as_stated: One additional patient per nurse increases odds of 30-day inpatient mortality by 7%
quality_note: Observational; shows coverage (presence) matters for care output

citation: Svartedalen nursing home six-hour day trial, Gothenburg 2015-17 (press reports; official evaluation not located)
design: Pilot, no formal evaluation read
estimate_as_stated: Press: ~14-17 extra staff hired; sick leave lower than city average; trial ended 2017
quality_note: News only; cost figures inconsistent across reports

citation: Gonzaga G. et al. (2003) Brazil 1988 reform; Varejao J. (2005) Portugal; Skuterud M. (2007) Quebec
url: (cited in Batut et al. 2023 literature review)
design: Various
estimate_as_stated: Described by Batut et al. as null employment/separation effects
quality_note: Not opened
